concept.name: CRDTs & Conflict-Free Replicated Data

relationships.description: Connects CRDTs & Conflict-Free Replicated Data to caching in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types) are replicated data structures whose concurrent updates commute or form a mathematical join-semilattice, guaranteeing every replica converges to the exact same state without coordination or consensus.
spark.keyTakeaway: CRDTs eliminate consensus round-trips for local-first apps and geo-distributed active-active stores by trading coordination latency for metadata overhead (vector clocks, tombstones, or per-element IDs).

concept.whyItMatters: Consensus protocols like Raft and Paxos require a quorum round-trip (50–150 ms across WANs) and stall during network partitions. Real-time collaborative editors (Figma, Notion/Linear-style local-first apps, Yjs, Automerge) and active-active distributed databases (Riak, Redis Enterprise Active-Active, Cassandra counters) need sub-millisecond local writes even offline. CRDTs mathematically guarantee **Strong Eventual Consistency (SEC)**: any two replicas that have received the same set of updates—in any order, with any duplicates—hold identical state.
whenToUse: Local-first collaborative applications (rich-text editors, whiteboards, offline-capable mobile apps) where edits must apply locally at 0 ms and merge cleanly upon reconnection.
Multi-region active-active databases tracking distributed counters, feature flags, shopping carts, or user presence sets without cross-region locks.
Edge/IoT telemetry aggregation where intermittent nodes push deltas over unreliable networks.
whenNotToUse: Strict global invariants such as preventing negative bank balances, enforcing unique usernames, or inventory reservation under scarcity (requires consensus or single-leader serialization).
Large binary blobs or relational joins that cannot be decomposed into monotonic state transitions.
Memory-constrained systems with high churn of deleted items where tombstone metadata cannot be garbage-collected.
keyPoints: State-based CRDTs (**CvRDTs**) ship full or delta state (`delta-CRDTs`) and merge via a **join-semilattice** operator `⊔` that is associative, commutative, and idempotent (ACID-free convergence).
Operation-based CRDTs (**CmRDTs**) ship small operations, requiring reliable causal broadcast (exactly-once or idempotent causal delivery) and commutative concurrent operations.

Core primitives include **G-Counter** (per-replica monotonic map), **PN-Counter** (two G-Counters for inc/dec), **LWW-Register** (timestamp + replicaId tie-breaker), and **OR-Set** (Observed-Remove Set using unique add-tags).
Sequence CRDTs (**RGA**, **YATA/Yjs**, **Fugue**) assign unique fractional/tree-ordered IDs to characters so concurrent insertions at the same cursor never interleave or corrupt text.
CRDTs guarantee *convergence*, not human *intention*—e.g., LWW-Register silently drops one concurrent write, and concurrent add+remove in an OR-Set resolves to add-wins or remove-wins by design.

examples.title: Real-Time Collaborative Rich Text via Yjs (YATA CRDT)
examples.scenario: 50 concurrent editors type, format, and paste offline/online in a shared browser document over WebSockets and WebRTC.
examples.outcome: Yjs encodes each character insertion with a `(clientId, clock)` ID and left/right origin pointers, merging 10,000+ out-of-order updates in <5 ms in-browser with zero central lock server.

examples.title: Active-Active Global Shopping Cart in Redis Enterprise
examples.scenario: Users in Mumbai and Frankfurt modify the same shopping cart across two active-active regional clusters during a transatlantic link flap.
examples.outcome: Using an Observed-Remove Set (OR-Set) CRDT with vector clocks, concurrent `add(SKU-A)` and `remove(SKU-B)` operations merge deterministically across regions once the link heals, avoiding lost cart items.

tradeOffs.pro: CvRDTs tolerate dropped, duplicated, and reordered messages over plain gossip/HTTP because `merge()` is idempotent and commutative.
tradeOffs.con: Shipping full state scales poorly with object size; delta-CRDTs mitigate this by shipping only recent state diffs.

tradeOffs.pro: Keeping tombstones (deleted item IDs) prevents 'zombie resurrection' when stale replicas sync late.
tradeOffs.con: Tombstones accumulate indefinitely in high-churn sets/documents unless compacted via causal stability barriers or epoch GC.

tradeOffs.pro: 100% write availability under network partitions (AP in CAP/PACELC) with 0 ms local write latency.
tradeOffs.con: Cannot enforce global uniqueness or non-negative bounds (e.g., `stock >= 0`) without adding a coordination layer.

failureModes.name: Clock Skew Corrupting LWW-Registers
failureModes.description: An LWW-Register using raw wall-clock `Date.now()` allows a replica with a 5-minute fast NTP clock to silently overwrite all newer edits from other nodes.
failureModes.mitigation: Use Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC) combining physical time with a monotonic logical counter and `replicaId` tie-breaker.

failureModes.name: Tombstone Bloat & OOM
failureModes.description: A collaborative document or OR-Set with millions of add/delete cycles grows 10x larger than its visible data because deleted elements remain as tombstones.
failureModes.mitigation: Run distributed garbage collection once all known replicas acknowledge a causal version vector, or compact via periodic epoch snapshots.

failureModes.name: Zombie Item Resurrection
failureModes.description: Pruning tombstones aggressively before an offline mobile client reconnects causes that client's stale state to re-introduce deleted items.
failureModes.mitigation: Never drop tombstones below the minimum causal frontier of active replicas, or force stale offline clients (>30 days) to re-bootstrap from a fresh snapshot.

failureModes.name: Replica ID Collisions
failureModes.description: Two browser tabs or cloned VMs share the same `replicaId` in a G-Counter or OR-Set, causing updates to overwrite each other and break convergence.
failureModes.mitigation: Generate a cryptographically random 64-bit/128-bit `clientId` per session/instance rather than reusing user IDs or hostnames.

commonMistakes: Using CRDTs to enforce invariants like 'only 1 seat left' or 'account balance cannot go below 0'—CRDTs cannot reject concurrent valid local writes.
Implementing a naive G-Counter keyed by `userId` instead of `replicaId`, which breaks when a user opens two tabs.
Assuming LWW-Register preserves all data—it explicitly discards losing concurrent writes.
Sending full CvRDT states on every keystroke instead of batching delta-CRDTs.
Forgetting to persist the local causal clock/vector alongside the CRDT state across restarts.

sections.content:
## The idea

Traditional replication relies on consensus (Raft/Paxos) to agree on a single global total order of writes. **CRDTs** invert the problem: instead of agreeing on *when* operations happened, design the data structure so that *order does not matter*.

Formally, a state-based CRDT (CvRDT) forms a **bounded join-semilattice** `(S, ⊔)`. Every local mutation moves the state monotonically upward in the partial order, and merging two replicas computes their least upper bound `A ⊔ B`. Because `⊔` is **associative** `(A ⊔ B) ⊔ C = A ⊔ (B ⊔ C)`, **commutative** `A ⊔ B = B ⊔ A`, and **idempotent** `A ⊔ A = A`, replicas can gossip updates over lossy, out-of-order networks and still converge identically.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace an **Observed-Remove Set (OR-Set)** with add-wins semantics across two disconnected replicas `R1` and `R2`:

1. **Initial state**: Both hold `{('milk', tag_1)}`. `R1` and `R2` go offline.
2. **`R1` removes `'milk'`**: `R1` moves `tag_1` into its `tombstones` set -> visible set is `{}`.
3. **`R2` concurrently removes and re-adds `'milk'`**: `R2` tombstones `tag_1` and generates a fresh unique tag `tag_2` -> visible set is `{('milk', tag_2)}`.
4. **Merge (`R1 ⊔ R2`)**:
   - `adds = {('milk', tag_1), ('milk', tag_2)}`
   - `tombstones = {tag_1}`
   - Visible elements = `adds \ tombstones` = `{('milk', tag_2)}`.

Unlike a naive set where `remove('milk')` would wipe out `R2`'s concurrent re-add, tagging each addition with a unique `(replicaId, seq)` ensures a remove only cancels the specific additions it *observed*.

sections.content:
## State-based vs. operation-based vs. delta

- **CvRDT (State-based)**: Replicas exchange full states and call `merge()`. Dead simple transport (works over plain HTTP polling or UDP gossip), but bandwidth is O(state size).
- **CmRDT (Op-based)**: Replicas broadcast tiny operations (e.g., `insert(pos, 'a')`). Low bandwidth, but requires **reliable causal broadcast** (no dropped or out-of-order ops).
- **Delta-state CRDTs (δ-CRDT)**: The modern sweet spot used in Riak, Yjs, and Automerge. Each mutation produces a small delta `δ` that is itself a valid CvRDT fragment. Replicas ship deltas and merge them idempotently, combining small payloads with loss-tolerant transport.

## Core CRDT catalog

| CRDT Type | Semantics | Metadata Overhead | Typical Use Case |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **G-Counter** | Increment-only counter | O(N replicas) integers | Distributed page views, rate counters |
| **PN-Counter** | Increment & decrement | 2 * O(N replicas) | Active user counts, inventory deltas |
| **LWW-Element-Set** | Add/remove via timestamps | O(items) + HLC timestamps | User profiles, config flags |
| **OR-Set** | Add-wins / remove-wins | O(adds) unique tags + tombstones | Shopping carts, collaborative tag lists |
| **YATA / RGA / Fugue** | Ordered text/list sequence | O(total chars incl. deleted) | Real-time collaborative text editors |

## Failure modes

1. **Wall-clock drift in LWW**: Relying on unsynchronized client clocks lets a skewed device win every conflict forever. *Fix*: Use Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC) bounded by server time.
2. **Unbounded tombstone growth**: High-churn documents accumulate megabytes of deleted character metadata. *Fix*: Run causal-barrier compaction when all peers acknowledge a version vector, or use run-length encoding (RLE) of contiguous IDs like Yjs/Automerge.
3. **Interleaving in naive sequence CRDTs**: Early sequence CRDTs (Logoot, LSEQ) could interleave two users' concurrently typed words (`hweolrldo`). *Fix*: Use modern non-interleaving algorithms like **Fugue** or **YATA**.
4. **Broken global invariants**: Two replicas concurrently decrementing a `PN-Counter` from 1 to -1 cannot be prevented locally. *Fix*: Use Escrow/Bounded-Counter patterns (pre-allocating per-replica quotas) or fall back to consensus for scarce resources.

## Compression & production libraries

Production CRDT engines avoid storing a JSON object per character:
- **Yjs**: Uses doubly-linked blocks (`Item` structs) with **ID run-length encoding**—typing `"hello"` creates 1 struct of length 5 instead of 5 structs, keeping memory ~1.5x raw text.
- **Automerge 2.0**: Stores columnar compressed change logs (inspired by Apache Arrow/Parquet) so a 100,000-edit document loads in ~10 ms and compresses 10x smaller than JSON.
- **Redis Enterprise CRDTs**: Implements native `G-Counter`, `PN-Counter`, `OR-Set`, and `LWW-Hash` inside C modules across active-active clusters.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Verify your domain does not require strict global invariants (e.g., uniqueness, non-negative stock).
- [ ] Assign a unique, persistent `replicaId` per client instance/tab—never reuse user IDs.
- [ ] Replace raw `Date.now()` with Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC) for any LWW conflict resolution.
- [ ] Use delta-CRDTs with run-length-encoded IDs (e.g., Yjs or Automerge) for sequences and large maps.
- [ ] Define a tombstone compaction / snapshot strategy before high-churn workloads hit memory limits.
- [ ] Fuzz-test `merge(A, B)` for associativity, commutativity, and idempotency under random network reordering.

interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on CRDTs & Conflict-Free Replicated Data. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Crdt Replicated Data Types

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types) are replicated data structures whose concurrent updates commute or form a mathematical join-semilattice, guaranteeing every replica converges to the exact same state without coordination or consensus.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Gossip / Delta Channel applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Join-Semilattice Merge (⊔).

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Join-Semilattice Merge (⊔) experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Use Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC) combining physical time with a monotonic logical counter and `replicaId` tie-breaker.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: CRDTs eliminate consensus round-trips for local-first apps and geo-distributed active-active stores by trading coordination latency for metadata overhead (vector clocks, tombstones, or per-element IDs).
Avoid trap: Using CRDTs to enforce invariants like 'only 1 seat left' or 'account balance cannot go below 0'—CRDTs cannot reject concurrent valid local writes.
Avoid trap: Implementing a naive G-Counter keyed by `userId` instead of `replicaId`, which breaks when a user opens two tabs.
When to reach for it: Local-first collaborative applications (rich-text editors, whiteboards, offline-capable mobile apps) where edits must apply locally at 0 ms and merge cleanly upon reconnection.
When to reach for it: Multi-region active-active databases tracking distributed counters, feature flags, shopping carts, or user presence sets without cross-region locks.

putItTogether.title: Putting Crdt Replicated Data Types Together
putItTogether.summary: CRDTs eliminate consensus round-trips for local-first apps and geo-distributed active-active stores by trading coordination latency for metadata overhead (vector clocks, tombstones, or per-element IDs).
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Crdt Replicated Data Types before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Yjs encodes each character insertion with a `(clientId, clock)` ID and left/right origin pointers, merging 10,000+ out-of-order updates in <5 ms in-browser with zero central lock server.
